items.text: States that a system classifying or predicting things makes two kinds of mistakes: false alarms and missed cases.
items.feedback_fail: Name the two mistake types plainly: false alarms (flagged but fine) and missed cases (real but not flagged).

items.text: Explains that reducing one kind of error usually increases the other, so every system chooses a balance.
items.feedback_fail: Add the trade-off: catching more real cases usually means more false alarms — every system picks a balance.

items.text: Gives a concrete example (e.g., spam filter, medical screening, fraud detection) naming what each error costs there.
items.feedback_fail: Use one concrete example and say what each kind of mistake costs in that situation.

items.text: Draws a practical consequence: no classifier is perfect, so important flagged or missed cases deserve human judgment.
items.feedback_fail: Close with the habit: no classifier is perfect, so important results deserve a person's judgment.

misconception_strings: a good model has no errors

anchors.pass_example: A spam filter makes two kinds of mistakes: false alarms, when a real email lands in spam, and missed cases, when spam reaches your inbox. Catching more spam usually means more real mail gets flagged — every system picks a balance. It is like airport security: stricter checks catch more but slow more innocent travelers. So no filter is perfect, and anything important deserves a human look.
anchors.fail_example: A good AI classifier is basically always right, and if it makes a mistake the engineers just fix it so it never happens again.
